title: Bounded local fibre-dimension locus is retrocompact
statement: Let $f:X\to S$ be a locally finitely presented morphism of schemes [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. For an integer $n\ge0$, let $U_n=\{x\in X\mid\dim_x(X_{f(x)})\le n\}$, where $X_{f(x)}$ is the scheme-theoretic fibre [def-pc-scheme-fibre] and the local dimension is the topological dimension at the corresponding point [def-kun-topological-dimension-at-point]. Then $U_n$ is an open subset of $X$ and is retrocompact in $X$ [def-weil-constructible-subset].

proof.text: First $f$ is locally of finite type: at every point, the locally-finite-presentation definition supplies an affine pair with a polynomial presentation in finitely many variables and finitely many relations. Its algebra is generated by the variable classes, so the pointwise locally-finite-type criterion applies. Apply the existing local-fibre-dimension openness theorem to $f$ and $n$. This proves that $U_n$ is open.

It remains to prove quasi-compactness of $U_n\cap W$ for every quasi-compact open $W\subset X$. For each $x\in W$, choose an affine open $V\subset S$ containing $f(x)$, then an affine open $U$ with $x\in U\subset W\cap f^{-1}(V)$, using the affine-open basis twice. Such $U$ cover $W$, and quasi-compactness of $W$ gives a finite subcover. Fix one such pair, write $U=\operatorname{Spec}B$, $V=\operatorname{Spec}R$, and denote the induced morphism by $h:U\to V$. By the fibre definition, the fibre of $h$ through $u\in U$ identifies topologically with the open subspace $U\cap X_{f(u)}$ of $X_{f(u)}$. Dimension at a point is unchanged on an open subspace. Thus $U\cap U_n$ is exactly the locus $L_n$ for $h$. It suffices to prove $L_n$ quasi-compact for this arbitrary affine pair.

The affine finite-presentation criterion says $R\to B$ is finitely presented. Apply the existing finite-presentation approximation theorem and choose any index in its nonempty directed system. Write $R_0\to B_0$ for that stage. Then $R_0$ is of finite type over $\mathbf Z$, $B_0$ is of finite type over $R_0$, and its clause (5) gives the compatible ring isomorphism $B_0\otimes_{R_0}R\cong B$. The affine fibre-product theorem therefore identifies $h:\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ with the base change of $h_0:\operatorname{Spec}B_0\to\operatorname{Spec}R_0$. Write $q:\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}B_0$ for the other projection.

proof.text: The ring $\mathbf Z$ is Noetherian directly from the ideal definition: a nonzero ideal contains a positive integer, and if $a$ is its least positive integer, division of any member by $a$ gives a remainder in the ideal between $0$ and $a-1$, hence remainder zero. Thus the ideal is $(a)$; the zero ideal is generated by $0$. Apply finite-type preservation of Noetherianity first to $\mathbf Z\to R_0$ and then to $R_0\to B_0$. Both $R_0$ and $B_0$ are Noetherian.

source.place: Tag 00FN (lemma-Noetherian-permanence), as used in the proof of Tag 00QJ

proof.text: The single affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}B_0$ has Noetherian section ring, so it is locally Noetherian by definition; it is quasi-compact because it is affine. The Noetherian-scheme closed-subset theorem gives the descending-chain condition on its closed subsets. Hence every subset is quasi-compact by the Noetherian-space compact-subsets theorem. In particular, the subset $L_{0,n}$ of points where the local fibre dimension of $h_0$ is at most $n$ is quasi-compact. It is also open: $B_0$ is a finite-type $R_0$-algebra, so the pointwise locally-finite-type criterion, using the whole source and target as an affine pair at each point, says $h_0$ is locally of finite type, and the local-fibre-dimension openness theorem applies to $h_0$ and $n$.

proof.text: For every $u\in\operatorname{Spec}B$, the base-change dimension theorem applied to the cartesian square of Step 3 gives equality of the local fibre dimensions of $h$ at $u$ and $h_0$ at $q(u)$. Its locally-finite-type hypothesis holds because $B_0$ is of finite type over $R_0$. Consequently $L_n=q^{-1}(L_{0,n})$ as subsets. The source of $q$ is affine and therefore quasi-compact, and its target is affine and therefore quasi-separated. The qcqs morphism permanence theorem implies that $q$ is quasi-compact. Since $L_{0,n}$ is a quasi-compact open by Step 5, the quasi-compact-preimage theorem proves that $L_n$ is quasi-compact.

proof.text: Return to the finite affine cover $W=U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_r$ in Step 2. Each $U_a\cap U_n$ is quasi-compact by Steps 3--6, and $W\cap U_n=\bigcup_{a=1}^r(U_a\cap U_n)$. Given an open cover of $W\cap U_n$, restrict it to each of these finitely many quasi-compact pieces and take a finite subcover for each; the union of the resulting finite families is a finite subcover of $W\cap U_n$. This also covers $r=0$. Thus $W\cap U_n$ is quasi-compact for every quasi-compact open $W$, which is exactly retrocompactness. Together with Step 1 this proves both assertions.
